name: Q and Not U
label: Dischord
lede: Q and Not U spent seven years trying to get D.C. punk crowds to dance, then quit while they were still climbing, leaving three albums on Dischord and one very colorful cover.

eras.title: Out of the ashes, into basements
eras.text: Several D.C. bands had broken up by the late '90s, and Q and Not U grew out of the pieces. They spent their first year in basements and living rooms, in a scene that had grown up on Dischord.

years.h: Four D.C. musicians start Q and Not U, and three of them sing
years.p: [[Chris Richards|0065280c-f561-4035-aa65-e9927988d72e]] and [[Harris Klahr|c788433e-623b-4e6c-8998-7c372b8d51b7]] play guitar and sing, [[John Davis|4729cedd-e42f-4836-8332-6cd316e60268]] sings and plays drums, and Matt Borlik plays bass.

years.h: Q and Not U play out for the first time
years.p: Dischord dates the band's first live shows to November 1998, a few months after they started practicing.
years.xp: Wikipedia puts the formation in summer 1998, with shows around D.C. starting that November.

years.h: A week of house shows turns into a coming-out party
years.p: Richards remembers four or five house shows in a week in the summer of 1999. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] takes notice, drawn to their musical language and the tight crowd forming around them.
years.xp: Richards told the Washington City Paper it felt like "the real coming-out party for the band."

eras.title: Thirty-one punks in primary colors
eras.text: Dischord put them out and MacKaye produced them. The cover of No Kill No Beep Beep became a group portrait of D.C. punk's next wave, then long tours followed and Borlik was out.

years.h: Hot and Informed · Dischord No. 123.5
years.p: Q and Not U's first single, a joint release by Dischord and DeSoto.

years.cap: The 31 on the cover shoot, George Washington University, Washington, D.C., August 2000
q: We were just waiting for some custodian to bust us.
years.h: Thirty-one kids in primary colors pose for the cover
years.p: Richards gathers 31 young D.C. punks, mostly under 25, in red, yellow and blue on the George Washington University campus. Shawn Brackbill shoots the picture for No Kill No Beep Beep.
years.xp: Nobody had asked permission. Richards told the City Paper the room spent the afternoon braced for a custodian.

years.cap: Q and Not U on stage at the Black Cat, Washington, D.C., 2000
years.h: No Kill No Beep Beep · Dischord No. 123
years.p: The debut, with MacKaye producing at [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear in about ten days. Jagged guitars, three voices trading lines, a rhythm section built to move people.
years.xp: The band had grown up on Dischord records and asked MacKaye to work with them. Wikipedia describes the record as strongly rhythmic, with dissonant guitar and bass over danceable beats.

years.h: Live in Washington DC, November 26, 2000

yt: Full show, Black Cat, Washington, D.C., November 26, 2000
years.h: Q and Not U spend 2001 on the road with friends
years.p: Long tours alongside [[Engine Down|65c54877-7b81-4cb1-8e6b-dc14fbec8b43]], [[Milemarker|151cbcfa-4618-4f26-a769-f15d33743262]], [[Ted Leo and the Pharmacists|31095622-5a1e-4f22-8ad1-b08eb6255f37]] and [[El Guapo|be23bf0a-67c6-4b2f-ba2a-89d983f5ebdd]].

years.cap: Bassist on stage at the Black Cat, Washington, D.C., 2000
years.h: Borlik is dismissed, and the band stays a trio
years.p: After two years of touring, Q and Not U let bassist Matt Borlik go, as Wikipedia puts it. Richards takes over the bass parts.
years.xp: Nobody was hired to replace him. The next two records were made by three people.

eras.title: A trio gets stranger
eras.text: Down to three, Q and Not U got bolder rather than smaller. They toured the U.S., Europe, Canada and Japan, and kept Dischord supplied with records.

years.h: On Play Patterns · Dischord No. 132
years.p: The first release from Q and Not U as a trio.

years.h: Different Damage · Dischord No. 133
years.p: The second album, made without a dedicated bass player, with Richards covering bass alongside guitar and vocals.

years.cap: Q and Not U as a trio, live, February 7, 2003
yt: X-Polynation, from the Burn to Shine D.C. film
years.h: X-Polynation and Book of Flags share a Dischord single
years.p: Two songs, Dischord No. 141, a year before the last album, Power.

eras.title: Make them dance, then stop
eras.text: Power went after the thing D.C. punk shows rarely had, which was dancing. A year later Q and Not U called it off while still climbing, with a statement that read more like a thank-you than a breakup.

years.h: Power, Dischord No. 143, is the last album
years.p: [[John Davis|4729cedd-e42f-4836-8332-6cd316e60268]] says that was the whole problem the band set out to solve on their third and final record.
years.xp: Davis told the City Paper: "No one ever danced at shows, so we wanted something that got people excited."

years.h: Live at the YWCA, Cambridge, 2004
"A beautiful and natural time" to stop, Q and Not U say
years.p: After seven years, the band says it has reached its shared goals, and hopes to play together again someday.
years.xp: The statement, as DCist printed it, said they had "reached all of our shared goals as Q and Not U." DCist called it another blow to the D.C. scene, coming after the Dismemberment Plan broke up.

years.cap: Q and Not U on the Siren Festival stage, Coney Island, July 16, 2005
years.h: Nine days after the news, a boardwalk stage at Coney Island
years.p: Q and Not U play the Siren Music Festival, one of their last shows outside D.C.

years.cap: Q and Not U at Fort Reno Park, Washington, D.C., July 18, 2005
yt: Fan footage, last Fort Reno show, July 18, 2005
years.h: A free Monday night at Fort Reno
years.p: The gig at D.C.'s summer park series was booked before the breakup news, and becomes one of the goodbyes.
years.xp: DCist listed the Fort Reno date as previously scheduled when it reported the breakup, with farewell D.C. shows for September still to be announced.

years.h: Wonderful People remix EP arrives as the band winds down
years.p: A Q and Not U remix EP comes out in September 2005.

yt: Soft Pyramids on Fox Rox, October 2003
years.h: Two nights at the Black Cat, and Soft Pyramids goes last
years.p: After finishing their touring, Q and Not U close with a Thursday and a Friday at the Black Cat on 14th Street. A fan commenting on Brooklyn Vegan wrote that it was a terrific show from an oddly underrated band.
years.xp: Fans who were there told Brooklyn Vegan that "Soft Pyramids" was the last song. setlist.fm logs only the September 23 show, so the Thursday date rests on those fan posts.

eras.title: The critic and the Paint Branch
eras.text: The three went their own ways. Davis went into pop with Georgie James and later Title Tracks, Klahr into his own projects in New York, and Richards into solo records as Ris Paul Ric and then the Washington Post. Richards and Davis ended up in a band together again.

years.h: Richards becomes the Washington Post's pop critic
years.p: Q and Not U's guitarist, bassist and cover-shoot organizer takes the beat.

years.h: Richards and Davis start [[Paint Branch|a440caa0-3fa8-4c39-9cd7-8fa0dffedd6e]]
years.p: The two former Q and Not U members form a new band, active through 2014 and listed on Dischord's Q and Not U page.

eras.title: The drummer keeps the files
eras.text: Davis became the keeper of the scene's paper trail, first as an archivist at the University of Maryland, where D.C. punk's zines and flyers live, and then as its historian.

years.h: The Post finds Davis among the collected papers at Maryland
years.p: The Washington Post profiles the Q and Not U drummer keeping D.C. punk alive at a University of Maryland library.

years.h: Davis launches Keep Your Ear to the Ground with MacKaye
years.p: His history of D.C. punk fanzines is launched at Politics and Prose in conversation with [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]], who produced Q and Not U's first album.
